content: Virola, also referred to as Epená, is a genus of medium-sized trees that are indigenous to the South American rainforest. These trees are closely related to other members of the Myristicaceae family, such as nutmeg. The Virola trees are characterized by their glossy, dark leaves and clusters of small yellow flowers, which emit a strong, pungent odor. The bark of the Virola tree produces a dark-red resin that contains several hallucinogenic alkaloids. Among these, the most notable are 5-MeO-DMT (found in Virola calophylla), 5-OH-DMT (commonly known as bufotenine), and N,N-DMT, which is considered one of the most potent compounds in the dimethyltryptamine family. Additionally, the resin contains beta-carboline harmala alkaloids, which act as monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) and significantly enhance the effects of DMT. The resin is traditionally prepared and dried using various methods, often involving the addition of ash or lime, which likely serve as alkalizing agents. A powder derived from the leaves of the Justicia bush is also commonly incorporated into the preparation. The resulting mixture is typically consumed through insufflation, a process similar to the use of Yopo. This involves an assistant blowing the powdered preparation through a long tube into the nostrils of the user. According to the ethnobotanist Richard Evans Schultes, the use of Virola in magico-religious rituals is primarily confined to certain indigenous tribes in the Western Amazon Basin and parts of the Orinoco Basin. In the context of traditional medicine, the tops of Virola oleifera have been found to produce lignan-7-ols and verrucosins, which exhibit antifungal properties. These compounds are effective against Cladosporium sphaerospermum at doses as low as 25 micrograms. Additionally, the lignan-7-ols oleiferin-B and oleiferin-G have demonstrated activity against Cladosporium cladosporioides at doses starting from 10 micrograms.
